profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a university-affiliated evidence synthesis center preparing a rapid methods pilot for an upcoming workshop on the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials. The team needs to decide how to split work for a small set of sample trial reports, produce a demonstration output for workshop attendees, and set a timeline for having materials ready before slides are finalized. The agenda is to confirm what materials will be prepared, who will assess the sample trials, how judgments will be documented, and when the draft package will be ready. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for extracting judgments from six example randomized trial reports, assembling a teaching handout, and delivering a draft 'bias summary' in time for workshop prep.

members.name: Dr. Priya Nandakumar
members.expertise: Systematic review methodology, trial appraisal, teaching evidence synthesis methods
members.background: Priya directs short-course content for an evidence synthesis center and has led multiple training workshops on trial quality assessment for clinicians and graduate students.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot materials to feel polished enough to reuse in future trainings, and she is worried that if the examples look messy or inconsistent, the workshop will undermine confidence in the center's methods teaching.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bias summary' for teaching naturally means a domain-level table showing each risk-of-bias domain judgment for every included trial.
When people say the materials should be 'ready by Monday,' they usually mean available in working draft form by Monday morning so slides can be built that day.
If the plan is to assess six sample trials, that normally means six full trial reports, with any companion protocol or supplement only consulted if attached to the same publication packet.
For a workshop demonstration, completing the assessments includes drafting one-sentence justifications for each domain so attendees can see how judgments are defended.

members.name: Evan Morales
members.role: Clinical Research Librarian and Review Support Specialist
members.expertise: Trial report retrieval, study packet assembly, evidence review workflows, documentation support
members.background: Evan supports review teams by locating trial records, compiling publication sets, and preparing structured evidence packets for appraisal exercises and rapid reviews.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the prep lightweight and feasible because he is also covering two other review teams this week, and he is concerned that overproducing documentation will create avoidable work.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bias summary' usually means the high-level graphic or color-coded overview shown in workshop materials, not a fully populated domain-by-domain evidence table.
When someone refers to materials being 'ready by Monday,' the default is end of day Monday unless a presentation starts earlier.
A 'trial' in preparation work typically refers to the complete study packet for one randomized comparison, including the main article, registry entry, protocol, and follow-up paper if available.
For internal workshop prep, the assessment is complete once each domain has a judgment label entered; detailed supporting quotes or rationale can be filled in later if needed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the bias summary
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce a 'bias summary' for the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a domain-level summary table with judgments and short supporting rationale for each trial across the standard Cochrane risk-of-bias domains.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a concise visual overview graphic or spreadsheet tab containing only the final high/low/unclear labels for each trial.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In evidence synthesis teams, 'bias summary' is a familiar phrase used for multiple artifacts, and both versions are plausible workshop outputs, so the term feels settled rather than in need of unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to split up the 'six trial reports' for assessment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of six main published trial articles, each treated as one item to appraise unless supplementary material happens to be attached.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of six study packets, where one 'trial report' may include multiple linked records such as the article, registry entry, protocol, and follow-up publication.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both often casually use 'trial report' to stand in for the study under review, and in planning talk neither needs to enumerate the packet contents, so the difference remains hidden.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that each assigned trial should be 'fully assessed' before handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'fully assessed' means every risk-of-bias domain has a judgment plus a short written rationale that can be directly shown to trainees.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'fully assessed' means every domain has a provisional judgment entered, even if rationale text is still missing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using standard workflow language from review practice, and because both imagine the other shares their default completion standard, neither sees a need to define the threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the draft package will be ready 'by Monday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means Monday morning, in time for her to build workshop slides and circulate a near-final teaching deck that afternoon.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means any time before close of business Monday, which is the normal interpretation for internal prep deadlines without a stated hour.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Internal planning meetings often use day-based deadlines as shorthand, and because no one explicitly mentions the workshop slide-building dependency, both hear the same deadline phrase as unambiguous.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pilot to look like something we could reuse in future trainings, not a rough internal exercise. For the workshop packet, the bias summary needs to read cleanly across the standard domains and include enough brief rationale that trainees can see how judgments are defended. And six trial reports should be manageable if we're just talking about six main trial articles rather than sprawling packets.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want us to leave with a clean plan for the risk-of-bias pilot: six trial reports, a bias summary for the teaching packet, and a straightforward path to getting the workshop materials into shape.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine as long as we keep it lightweight. I can pull together six study packets in the shared folder and make sure each trial report has the linked records with it, because that usually prevents back-and-forth later. If we're just aiming for a concise bias summary, this should be very doable.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can get the six trial reports organized in a shared folder and label everything clearly. If we decide who owns which ones now, the bias summary should come together pretty smoothly.

turns.inner_thought: Three each is fair. I need every assigned article fully assessed before we merge, meaning all domains judged and each one has a short sentence explaining the call so I can drop it straight into teaching materials. If we don't hold that line, the handout will look thin.
turns.utterance: Why don't we split them evenly? I can assess three and you can assess three, and we can make sure each assigned trial is fully assessed before we merge everything into the workshop set.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I can front-load some of the retrieval work and bundle the linked records so entering the judgments goes faster. For me, fully assessed just means every domain has a label in place before handoff; we can always flesh things out later if Priya wants more text.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I can pre-load the study packets with the linked records so each assessment moves faster once we start entering judgments.

turns.inner_thought: I should signal that this has to teach, not just document. The bias summary needs to let attendees read across domains and see why a judgment landed where it did. If it's only labels, it won't support the discussion well and it won't feel polished enough to reuse.
turns.utterance: Great. I do want the bias summary to be easy for attendees to read across domains and still useful when we're explaining why each judgment was made.

turns.inner_thought: She's emphasizing readability, which fits a compact overview. I can make a tidy summary sheet with consistent labels and probably color-code it so it works in the handout. As long as all the judgments are entered cleanly, that should be enough for internal workshop prep.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I can set up a compact summary sheet and make sure all the judgments are entered consistently for the handout.

turns.inner_thought: I need to flag the timing without overcomplicating it. By Monday should be enough for anyone to understand I need it in hand Monday morning so I can build slides that day and circulate the deck in the afternoon. If I get it later, slide prep becomes rushed.
turns.utterance: On timing, I only need the draft package by Monday so I can fold the examples into the slide deck without rushing the workshop prep.

turns.inner_thought: Monday is workable if we're talking end of day, even with the two other review teams I'm covering. I'll have my three study packets assembled and my judgments entered once I get through what's already in my queue. Good—this stays feasible.
turns.utterance: Monday works on my side. I should have my half wrapped once I finish assembling the trial materials already on my queue.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want us getting bogged down chasing missing details across multiple sources for a teaching example. If a main article is sparse, we can still use it as the basis for the exercise rather than treating extra records as required to proceed.
turns.utterance: And if one article is a bit thin on methods, that's okay—we can still keep moving and use the published report as the basis for the workshop example.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. I'll still add registry or protocol links with the reports because that's part of a proper packet and helps make the assessment complete on my end, even if she mainly works from the article. It doesn't mean I need to write out full rationales right away.
turns.utterance: That's fine. I'll include any registry or protocol links alongside the reports so the assessments are complete on my end.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll review the merged bias summary Monday morning and turn it into the final handout after I clean up wording and align the one-line justifications. If the draft is solid enough, this could become a reusable template for future methods teaching.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll review the merged bias summary on Monday and then turn it into the final workshop handout.

turns.inner_thought: So I own three study packets, I'll set up the shared folder, and I'll deliver a completed draft by Monday—meaning before close of business. If I keep the output to clean judgments and organized materials, I can get this done without creating a lot of extra documentation.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll take ownership of three trial reports, get the shared folder set up, and send over the completed draft by Monday.
